The early life stages of Cisco (Coregonus artedi) begin with a fertilised egg that undergoes progressive yolk absorption within the chorion. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva emerges, carrying an endogenous nutrient reserve that sustains it through the lecithotrophic phase until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. The wet weight at birth is 0.0039 grams [Wwb = 0.0039 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of approximately 1.95 millimeters, which yields a spherical volume that dictates the initial hatchling mass. This modest starting mass reflects the relatively small egg size characteristic of coregonines. The newly emerged alevin remains non-feeding for a brief interval, during which it relies entirely on its yolk stores before transitioning to active prey capture. The point at which the yolk is fully resorbed and the exotrophic transition is complete marks a critical developmental window, after which the free-swimming larva must locate suitable planktonic prey to sustain its rapid growth trajectory.

As juvenile Cisco progress through the summer growing season, they undergo a pronounced allometric shift that accompanies the larval-juvenile transition. Body length increases steadily, and by the time individuals approach puberty, females typically reach a total length of 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters], with some locally reported variation extending from 28 to 34 centimeters. This size at sexual maturation is a key demographic parameter, as it determines the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the initiation of reproductive activity. The mass of a female at this developmental stage is approximately 145.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 145.6 grams], representing a substantial increase from the birth mass achieved through months of intensive feeding on zooplankton. This relationship between length and mass follows a power-law scaling common to many freshwater teleosts, consistent with regional growth models derived from lake survey data. The attainment of puberty is thus tightly linked to both linear size and body condition, with slower-growing individuals delaying their first spawning event.

Adult Cisco in many Laurentian Great Lakes populations exhibit a maximum recorded total length of 57 centimeters [Li = 57 centimeters]. Individuals reaching this ultimate size have achieved their asymptotic length, after which somatic growth slows considerably and nearly ceases. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for such a specimen is approximately 1,950 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,950 grams], a mass that reflects the considerable accumulation of muscle and lipid reserves typical of a long-lived, iteroparous fish. This maximum body mass is achieved only by the oldest and most successful individuals in a cohort, as growth rates decline with age due to the increasing investment of resources toward reproduction and meeting daily metabolic costs. Field surveys of spawning aggregations indicate that only a small fraction of the population attains this exceptional size, with most adults falling well below the asymptotic values. The large body size confers advantages in fecundity and competitive ability on the spawning grounds.

The reproductive biology of Cisco is characterized by a single annual spawning event each autumn, when adults congregate over shallow reefs and shoals to release their gametes. Females produce a large number of oocytes per spawning event, with the fecundity per reproductive event estimated at approximately 24,549 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 24,549 eggs per clutch]. Given that a female typically spawns just one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], the annual reproductive output is considerable, though it is heavily dependent on adult body size and condition. Under the thermal regime typical of their native habitat, with a stable water temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the metabolic costs of vitellogenesis and gamete maturation are met through the mobilization of stored lipids acquired during the preceding summer foraging period. This strategy aligns with that of many cold-water iteroparous salmonids that invest heavily in a single, high-fecundity spawning event rather than multiple, smaller clutches across a season.

Longevity records for wild Cisco indicate a maximum lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] for individuals inhabiting cooler, oligotrophic lakes where metabolic demands are reduced at a temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. At 11 °C [T = 11 °C], these fish experience a relatively slow pace of life, with sustained somatic growth across many seasons before senescence eventually sets in. The oldest documented individuals are typically those from deep, cold-water refugia where predation pressure is low and food resources are stable across years. This extended lifespan, combined with iteroparous reproduction, allows older females to contribute disproportionately to the next generation through their larger clutch sizes. Following the completion of their final spawning, natural mortality ensues from progressive physiological deterioration and post-reproductive senescence, a pattern that ensures the species maintains stable population dynamics across variable environmental conditions.
